EFL in the Community

What is EFL in the community?

Established in 2008, EFL in the Community is the charitable arm of the English Football League (EFL) and uses the power of sport to improve people’s lives with the vision to create stronger, healthier, more active communities across the country.

It resources the network of EFL Club Community Organisations - the charities linked to each EFL Club.

Focusing on improving health and wellbeing, raising aspirations, and realising potential and building stronger, more cohesive communities, the network engages with over 840,000 participants each year and generates a total of £865million of social value across the full range of community initiatives and programmes.

Objectives

Since 2023, EFL in the Community has prioritised developing programmes to support refugee and people seeking asylum communities within the footprint of their 72 Community Club Organisations (CCOs). Their goal is to create a suite of national programmes that harness football’s global appeal to engage refugees and people seeking asylum in positive activities.

They recognise that sport participation improves physical and mental health while helping those in disadvantaged communities feel more connected to their local area, enhancing community cohesion and understanding.

Their future objectives include:

Increasing refugee and people seeking asylum participation in EFL in the Community programmes.

Developing sustainable funded projects in high-need areas, enabling more EFL CCOs to deliver targeted programmes.

Creating a centrally funded offer for multiple CCOs to enhance engagement and support for refugees and people seeking asylum.

Fostering connectedness between refugees, people seeking asylum, and local communities through programmes that bring diverse groups together.

Improving mental health and physical activity levels among refugee and people seeking asylum communities.

Leveraging football’s media coverage to showcase sport’s positive impact on refugee and people seeking asylum communities, developing case studies to promote understanding and challenge negative stereotypes.

Using football engagement to create training, education, and employment opportunities, empowering refugees, and people seeking asylum to build brighter futures.

Delivery

Centrally, EFL in the Community is piloting and developing programmes that support refugees and people seeking asylum. In June 2024, in partnership with UNHCR it developed the Stronger Communities Cup, a football competition designed to bring refugees and non-refugees together, using the power of football as a tool to break down barriers and develop friendships. This programme was showcased by UEFA as part of the Champions League Final celebrations in London.

The Stronger Communities Cup programme was developed further in October 2024 as a week-long residential programme, that not only combines a football competition for refugees and people seeking asylum but includes a residential programme designed to not only bring people together from across the country, but also develop key leadership skills such as resilience, team building and confidence.

EFL in the Community has also developed a small pilot programme in partnership with the Football Association and UEFA, working with young refugees and people seeking asylum, supporting them to become future community sports leaders. This 6-month programme has 20 refugees and people seeking asylum attending workshops focusing on confidence, mental health, teamwork, listening skills and resilience. The ambition is for this to expand in 2025.

Sheffield Wednesday FC Community Programme are one of just a handful of CCOs currently working directly with an accommodation provider (Mears Housing), delivering weekly football sessions and football tournaments across Yorkshire. SWFCCP engage with roughly 15 – 20 people per week and the focus is to provide physical activity sessions as a way of settling and feeling welcomed within Sheffield.

Evidence of impact of EFL in the community

Sheffield Wednesday have reported great physical benefits for the people that engage with EFL in the Community, many have taken up running as a hobby, as well as attending wider football sessions across Sheffield. The programme is very transient, with people leaving the city frequently, however this short-term provision has allowed them to settle and reduce anxiety by supporting them to feel welcome and part of something in their local community.

Challenges

One of the biggest challenges faced by the network currently is inconsistency of funding. All funding currently is delivered at a local level, but often does not allow CCOs to deliver a consistent year long programme, with some CCOs only able to deliver programmes for a few months per year.

Replicability and scalability

EFL in the Community has a network of 72 CCOs that provides support to communities in almost every area of England and Wales. EFL in the Community has an infrastructure in place that supports the growth of new and existing provision throughout the network, and has robust mechanism relating governance, safeguarding, and data management, which has been built through the delivery of national government programmes such as the National Citizen Service as well as corporate partnership programmes such as Kellogg’s Football Camps.

About this document

This document provides an overview of the workstreams, resources and case studies developed or endorsed by the Home Office Asylum Mental Health and Wellbeing (MHW) team. The aim is to raise awareness about what is available and highlight examples of good practice measures, to support people seeking asylum’s mental health and wellbeing. All workstreams outlined in this booklet have either been clearly delineated as localised pilots with aspirations for rollout or available UK wide. In both instances, the MHW team believe that they will be of interest to stakeholders right across the UK.

Similarly, whilst case studies may highlight local initiatives, they are shared to inspire fresh action and partnership across all nations.

In the next iteration of this booklet, we hope to be able to showcase new case studies. If you would like to highlight good practice via this platform, we would welcome any fresh examples for inclusion at tip@homeoffice.gov.uk.

Introduction

The Asylum Mental Health & Wellbeing (MHW) team has a priority focus on leading the conversation around healthcare, mental health and general wellbeing of people seeking asylum. The team lead on a wide range of engagement strands and delivery of programmes across the asylum environment, always focussing on partnership working to maximise opportunities for growth.

Taking preventative measures to reduce potential negative impacts on the mental health and wellbeing of people seeking asylum, the team progress activity in four distinct parts:

provision of training and practical tools to upskill colleagues and partners.

sharing good practice.

commissioning services and research to plug gaps in services and evidence where possible; and

development of effective partnerships with health, voluntary sector, and local authority stakeholders to deliver appropriate care pathways for people seeking asylum.

Trauma-Informed Practice (TIP)

Overview

Recognising the prevalence of trauma amongst people seeking asylum in their home country, on route and upon arrival in the UK, the MHW team has developed a workstream from concept to implementation to embed TIP by:

supporting change towards a culture that seeks to recognise, respond to signs of trauma, and reduce the risk of further distress and re-traumatisation of people seeking asylum.

supporting the reduction of the risk of vicarious trauma of Home Office colleagues and contracted partners.

establishing a strong connection between TIP training and day-to-day process, culture and thinking.

helping strengthen the referral process for safeguarding and/or trauma-related issues.

The aim is that through a greater knowledge about and confidence in identifying signs of trauma, colleagues will use more trauma sensitive language, enact more trauma sensitive behaviours, and create more trauma-informed referral processes and physical environments.

The MHW team conducted an end-to-end asylum journey review in conjunction with clinical partner, Hedroc, in March 2023. The team drew upon clinical and lived experience expertise to inform provision of training and resources to engender culture change across the Home Office and its partners.

Alongside Hedroc, the MHW team onboarded CDS Support as their L&D partner to design and deliver a learning programme for colleagues, comprising of the following modules:

TIP Awareness.

TIP Leadership.

TIP Skilled.

TIP Policy and Communications.

TIP Physical Environment.

TIP Working in Partnership with Lived Experience; and

TIP Signposting.

These modules take the form of digital self-led training with supplementary discussion guides, practical tools, and wider sustainability mechanisms now all sitting together on an internal TIP Information Hub. Learning journeys for colleagues are determined by their degree of impact upon and contact with people seeking asylum.

The MHW team has consistently worked in partnership with lived experience groups including Home Office and Migrant Help Asylum Lived Experience Advisory Panels (ALEAPs) as well as Survivors Speak Out to ensure the voices of those with lived experience of seeking asylum in the UK are heard.

The MHW team contracted Revealing Reality to evaluate the pilots which informed the development of final training products.

Evidence of impact of Refugee Radio

90% of participants reported positive wellbeing indicators after participating in the mental-health support group.

Challenges

The mental health support group works best when it can be offered as a complementary to 1-2-1 trauma therapy, rather than an alternative. However, there is a gap between primary and secondary care, so the needs of asylum seekers and refugees with PTSD are often deemed too severe for primary care but if they are not actively suicidal, they are unable to access secondary care services. NHS funding and care pathways are required to plug this gap in provision.

Where funding has been secured to pay for long-term 1-2-1 trauma therapy such as EMDR, this has delivered the best results alongside the project.

Replicability and scalability

Mental-health support groups were piloted in Eastbourne and Hastings in response to the opening of S98 initial accommodation in those areas. Section 98 support provides accommodation for people seeking asylum who would otherwise be destitute and who are either awaiting a decision on an application for Section 95 support or are supported under Section 95 and are awaiting transfer to their accommodation.

The model established in Brighton would need to be replicated in areas to which people seeking asylum are dispersed. Dispersal accommodation is longer-term temporary accommodation managed by accommodation providers on behalf of the Home Office.

The specialist advice and casework service would need to be provided alongside the groups to ensure the project is holistic. Otherwise, participants would become overwhelmed by structural issues and may disengage with the therapeutic offer.

Improving Volunteering and Recruitment Pathways for Asylum Seekers and Refugees, Bath, Swindon and Wiltshire (BSW)

What is Volunteering and Recruitment Pathways for Refugees, BSW?

Great Western Hospital Foundation Trust is an anchor institute and collaborates with different projects in the community. The Trust has been working with the Harbour Project for the past eight years.

Objectives

The Harbour Project is a voluntary sector organisation set up to help asylum seekers and refugees rebuild their lives and connect with organisations within the local community to access voluntary roles.

Delivery

In 2023 the Trust employed 20-25 volunteers from the Harbour Project. Most of these volunteers were asylum seekers living in contingency hotels.

The Trust conducts DBS checks using a Declaration Enhanced Disclosure Questionnaire, which is reviewed every three years. Occupational Health checks are also carried out with English language tests and a Trust induction is undertaken by new volunteers.

Volunteers provide a minimum of three hours per week working within the Trust. The main voluntary roles on offer include:

Patient befrienders, who give help and support to patients including tea & coffee rounds and completing pharmacy runs.

Outpatient welcome liaison service volunteers, who meet and greet patients, helping them to their appointments if have mobility issues.

Evidence of impact

Many asylum seekers volunteering through the programme have previous clinical skills and knowledge which are beneficial to the Trust. The Trust tries to link an individual’s skill sets/areas of interest to the work they do. For example, a volunteer who is a trained physiotherapist is helping the Physiotherapy Team.

Recruiting asylum seekers from contingency hotels into voluntary positions within the local community has helped to improve the wellbeing of vulnerable individuals who are not able to obtain paid employment in the UK, as they have not yet been granted Leave to Remain status.

Many volunteers from the programme have gone on to apply for full time, paid employment with the Trust following their Leave to Remain being granted.

The project has led to full time paid employment for some volunteers once they have had their Leave to Remain granted.

New project funding was granted to purchase equipment for meaningful activities with patients such as arts and crafts. Volunteers can now hold sessions with patients during their recovery.

The development of the Declaration Enhanced Disclosure Questionnaire has reduced the burden of obtaining references from employers for migrants, refugees and asylum seekers who are unable to complete a DBS. It is recognised that it can be inappropriate to request evidence of past employment from countries experiencing conflict.

Challenges

Travelling to work in the hospital has been an issue for volunteers and the cost of this had presented as a barrier to employment. The trust has hired a Transport Coordinator to support the hub project. Volunteers can now claim expenses for transport by completing an expense form and providing bus tickets to the cashier’s office to refund the cost.

DBS checks are tailored to UK residents and request references from someone living in the UK who has known the person for more than two years. This can be difficult for asylum seekers recently arriving to the country. This led to the development of the ten question Declaration Enhanced Disclosure Questionnaire for those who can only provide an residence card which they must complete and sign before starting a volunteer position.
